title: Progressive Judaism worldwide
hookLine: Liberal and Progressive movements in Britain, Europe, Israel and beyond

cards: Three signs on three synagogue doors. One, in London, says Liberal. One, in Tel Aviv, says Progressive, in Hebrew.
One, in an American suburb, says Reform.
Step through any of them on a Friday night and some things will feel familiar: Hebrew and the local language side by side, women and men leading together, a sermon that might quote Amos.
Some will feel different: the tunes, the accents, how much Hebrew, what's for dinner after. Three names on three doors. Are they three movements, or one?

teach.b: Progressive Judaism worldwide. Progressive is the family name. In different countries the family members have different first names, and they are linked through an international union of Progressive congregations.

Two movements grew up there side by side, one called Reform and one called Liberal. Liberal Judaism in Britain grew partly through the work of Lily Montagu, who helped found it and led services herself.
The two, each with its own prayer books and rabbis, have been drawing closer under the Progressive name. Second, Europe.
On the continent, some congregations call themselves Liberal and some Progressive, and they pray in Hebrew and in their own languages, from Paris to Berlin to Amsterdam. Third, Israel.
There the movement calls itself Progressive Judaism, in Hebrew yahadut mitkademet. Its congregations pray in Hebrew as a matter of course, so the question of how much Hebrew simply disappears.
Like Masorti communities, they build their life alongside an official rabbinate that is Orthodox. What do the doors share?
The ideas from this week: ethics at the center, informed choice, women and men as equals, and the prophets' call.

teach.h: AN HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.
teach.b: And a verse some of these communities like to quote, from Isaiah: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Each country has its own door, and its own name on it.
The house behind the doors is shared.

how: Progressive Jews around the world belong to congregations called Reform, Liberal or Progressive, linked through an international union; they pray in Hebrew and local languages and share commitments to ethics, informed choice and equality.

o: an Israeli group pushing for faster changes in the law
a newer movement that replaced Reform across Europe
one family of Reform, Liberal and Progressive Jews worldwide

games.q: you're opening a Progressive congregation in a new country. what goes on the sign?
o: whatever name fits the place: Reform, Liberal or Progressive.
games.why: each country has its own name on the door: Reform in America, Reform and Liberal in Britain, Liberal or Progressive in Europe, Progressive in Israel. the house behind the doors is shared.

practice: Say the three names slowly, Reform, Liberal, Progressive, and let each sit for a breath: what does each one lean toward, change, freedom, moving forward?
Then think of a name you yourself go by in different places, at home, at work, with old friends. Same person, different door.

wordCard.voice: Progressive Judaism worldwide. One family with many names: Reform, Liberal, Progressive, linked across Britain, Europe, Israel and beyond. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Progressive Judaism, the name the movement uses in Israel.

carryVoice: Your line: worldwide. Many names on the doors, one house behind them. See you tomorrow.
